title: Glossary
summary: Regulatory language is precise, and its precision is where the meaning lives. These are the terms that appear across the platform, defined as the instruments define them.

terms.definition: Replacement, Reduction, and Refinement — the framework set out by Russell and Burch in 1959 that structures nearly all law and policy on animal use in science. Replacement removes animals from a procedure; Reduction lowers the number used; Refinement lessens suffering within a procedure that still uses them.

A structured description of the causal chain running from a molecular initiating event, through key intermediate events, to an adverse effect in an organism. AOPs are what make targeted in vitro assays a scientifically defensible replacement for a whole-animal test.
The date after which a certified company commits that no animal testing has occurred anywhere in its supply chain. A fixed cut-off date is auditable. A claim written only in the present tense is not.

A procedure developed at the US FDA in 1944 in which a substance is applied to the eye or shaved skin of a restrained rabbit and the resulting damage scored over days. It is the test that in vitro reconstructed tissue methods were built to replace, and the reason ‘rabbit’ became the visual shorthand for this entire subject.

The specific biological effect a test is designed to detect — skin irritation, eye damage, sensitisation, genotoxicity, repeated-dose toxicity. Bans and exemptions are almost always written endpoint by endpoint, which is why blanket statements about testing being ‘banned’ so often mislead.
The formulated cosmetic as sold. A claim that a finished product was not tested on animals says nothing about its individual ingredients, which is where testing overwhelmingly occurs.

Under China's CSAR, the category covering ordinary products such as most cleansers, moisturisers, and colour cosmetics. Since May 2021, imported general cosmetics may qualify for exemption from pre-market animal testing under specified conditions.
Performed by computational modelling rather than in a living organism or in culture. Includes QSAR models and physiologically based kinetic simulation.
Performed outside a living organism — in cell culture, reconstructed tissue, or isolated tissue preparations.
Performed in a living organism. In this context, an animal test.

A prohibition on placing a product on the market where it relies on animal test data, as distinct from a prohibition on carrying out the test. The EU marketing ban is what gives its regime extraterritorial force: a company cannot test elsewhere and sell in Europe.

Any technology, methodology, or combination of approaches that provides information on chemical hazard and risk without using animals. Deliberately broader than ‘alternative test’, because most replacements are combinations rather than single tests.

An exposure-led, hypothesis-driven framework for reaching a safety decision using in vitro bioactivity data, computational models, and existing knowledge, without generating new animal data. The leading approach for systemic endpoints that no single test replaces.

An internationally agreed testing method adopted by the OECD. Data generated under a Test Guideline must be accepted by all member countries under Mutual Acceptance of Data, which is what converts a validated method into a usable regulatory tool.

The corporate owner of a brand. A brand may hold a certification while its parent sells other brands in markets requiring animal testing. Whether that matters is an ethical judgement, not a factual one — but it cannot be made without knowing the ownership.

A computational model of how a substance is absorbed, distributed, metabolised, and excreted, used to translate an external dose into an internal concentration at the tissue of interest. The bridge between an in vitro result and a real-world exposure.

Testing conducted by a regulator on products already on sale, as opposed to testing required before approval. Relevant to China, where removing a pre-market requirement did not remove the authority to test after launch.

Regulation (EC) No 1907/2006 on the Registration, Evaluation, Authorisation and Restriction of Chemicals. It governs substances as chemicals rather than as cosmetic ingredients, and can require animal data for worker or environmental safety even where cosmetics law forbids testing for cosmetic purposes.
Predicting a substance's properties from data on structurally similar substances. A well-justified read-across avoids generating new data of any kind.
A three-dimensional model of human skin grown from donated keratinocytes, differentiated to resemble living epidermis. The basis of the adopted replacements for skin corrosion and irritation testing.

Harm arising from exposure over an extended period rather than a single dose. Historically assessed in 28- or 90-day rodent studies; the endpoint where full replacement remains hardest and where honest accounts should say so.
The capacity of a substance to induce an allergic response on repeated skin contact. Now assessable without animals by combining assays that each measure one key event in the adverse outcome pathway.

Under China's CSAR, categories subject to stricter approval — hair dyes, perming products, freckle-removing and whitening products, sunscreens, anti-hair-loss products, and products making new efficacy claims. These remain subject to animal testing requirements.

The study of how a substance moves through the body over time. One of three endpoints for which the EU marketing ban was deferred from 2009 to 2013, on the grounds that no replacement was then available.

The formal process of establishing that a test method is reliable and relevant for a defined purpose, conducted by bodies such as EURL ECVAM and ICCVAM. Validation, not laboratory demonstration, is what makes a method usable in a regulatory submission — and it is why the gap between ‘a replacement exists’ and ‘a replacement is accepted’ can run to years.
